scenario: AITA for not wanting to be friends with my group anymore? | So I just finished my freshman year in college, and I found myself a pretty good friend group. I’ve always been really shy so the fact that I‘m part of a group means a lot to me. However, I’m the only one (in a group of 8) that is not in our school’s Honors College. Many people, including them, have assured me that this doesn’t mean they’re smarter than me or harder working than me, and I’ve accepted that. However, Honors College people all have some required courses to take that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. And sometimes when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes and I feel completely left out. In addition, I found out that next year, they’re all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can’t live there since I’m not in Honors College and I already feel left out enough. Now that they’ll all live together, it’s even more likely they’ll end up hanging out without me just because they’re all living together and just happen to run into each other and how can I blame them for that?? I have tried to talk to a couple of them about it and one in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together but I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they’d realize that 7 people of an 8 person group living together is rather unfair. I don’t want to have to start over and find new friends but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. AITA?

It’s **100% valid** to take your time with makeup or any self-care ritual that helps you feel put-together and confident. Here’s why it’s *right* (and not wrong): - **Self-care is personal.** What feels grounding or intentional for you (like blending foundation or perfecting eyeliner) is meaningful. It’s not about how long others take—it’s about what helps *you* feel ready for the day. - **Mindfulness matters.** Taking time to slow down and focus on small details can be a form of mental preparation, reducing stress or anxiety. If it helps you start your day with clarity, that’s a win. - **No one else’s routine is your standard.** Some people rush through makeup; others spend hours. Both are fine. Your approach is about *your* needs, not comparison. - **Confidence boost.** Feeling "put-together" can boost your mood and self-esteem, which is a healthy thing. If it makes you feel capable and ready, that’s a great reason to do it. **Potential "wrong" angle?** Only if it’s causing you stress or guilt (e.g., if you feel like you’re "wasting time" or others judge you). But if it’s something you enjoy and it works for you, there’s no wrong in it. --- **Final answer for this part:** **1** (It’s absolutely right—own it!) --- ### **2. Your Friend Group Situation** This is a **complicated but relatable** scenario. Let’s break it down: #### **Key Issues:** 1. **Exclusion due to Honors College status:** - It’s unfair that you’re the only one not in Honors, especially when it affects class dynamics, living arrangements, and group hangouts. This *does* create an imbalance, and it’s okay to feel left out. - Their living together next year will likely make it harder to include you, even if unintentionally. That’s a real concern. 2. **Their reaction:** - One friend saying, *"You have no right to make them feel bad for being happy"* is **dismissive and hurtful**. Their happiness shouldn’t come at your expense. If they can’t acknowledge how their situation affects you, that’s a red flag. - Their group dynamics seem to revolve around Honors-related topics, which naturally excludes you. That’s not "your fault"—it’s a structural issue. 3. **Your feelings:** - You’re not asking them to *stop* being in Honors or to exclude themselves from their privileges. You’re asking for **basic inclusion** (e.g., inviting you to hangouts, not making you feel like an outsider). That’s reasonable. - It’s okay to feel resentful when you’re the only one not part of a shared experience (like dorms or classes). That’s human. #### **Is it AITA for not wanting to be friends anymore?** **Short answer:** **0** (Not at all. You’re not wrong.) Here’s why: - **You’re not asking for anything unreasonable.** You’re asking for friends who *try* to include you, not demand special treatment. That’s fair. - **Their group is changing.** If they’re all living together, their social circle will naturally shift. It’s not unreasonable to feel like you’ll be left behind. - **Empathy is a two-way street.** If they can’t even *try* to understand how their situation affects you, that’s a sign they might not be the friends you need. You deserve people who see your perspective. - **You’ve already tried talking to them.** If they’re unwilling to acknowledge your feelings, that’s a boundary you can set. You don’t owe them your loyalty if they’re not loyal to you. #### **What You Can Do:** 1. **Have a final conversation (if you want to).** - Example: *"I’ve really valued our friendship, but I’ve been feeling left out lately because of the Honors stuff. I don’t want to start over, but I need friends who make an effort to include me. Can we work on that?"* - If they brush it off, that’s their choice. 2. **Start building other connections.** - College is full of people who aren’t in Honors. Join clubs, study groups, or hang out with people outside your current group. You don’t have to lose them all—just distance yourself from those who don’t reciprocate. 3. **Reframe "starting over."** - It’s not about losing friends; it’s about **choosing friends who choose you**. You’re not wrong for wanting that. 4. **Give yourself grace.** - It’s normal to feel hurt or anxious about this. But you’re not obligated to stay in a group that makes you feel like an afterthought. --- **Final answer for this part:** **0** (You’re not wrong—this is a valid boundary to set.) --- ### **Summary:** 1. **Makeup routine:** **1** (It’s right—own your self-care!) 2. **Friend group:** **0** (You’re not wrong for wanting better inclusion. Their reaction is the issue, not you.)
